```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  out.width = "100%"
)
```

Every business day B3, the Brazilian exchange, publishes the `PRE` curve: the
fixed rate (pre-fixed) yield curve in BRL, with rates for hundreds of
maturities.
The curve is built from the settlement prices of the DI1 futures, and the
rates between two DI1 maturities are interpolated with the flat forward
method: the forward rate is constant between two vertices.

In this article we build a curve from the DI1 futures only, interpolate it
with `interp_flatforward()`, and compare it with the curve that B3 publishes.

```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(fixedincome)
```

## The data

Both curves are downloaded with the
[rb3](https://github.com/wilsonfreitas/rb3) package.
`yc_brl_get()` returns the curve published by B3 and
`yc_brl_with_futures_get()` returns the same curve with the DI1 contract of
each maturity.
The DI1 curve is the first vertex of B3's curve (one business day, the
overnight rate) plus the vertices of the DI1 contracts.

```{r eval=FALSE}
library(rb3)
library(dplyr)

refdate <- as.Date("2026-09-11")
fetch_marketdata("b3-reference-rates", refdate = refdate, curve_name = "PRE")
fetch_marketdata("b3-futures-settlement-prices", refdate = refdate)

b3 <- yc_brl_get() |>
  filter(refdate == !!refdate) |>
  collect() |>
  select(refdate, forward_date, biz_days, r_252) |>
  filter(!is.na(r_252)) |>
  arrange(biz_days)

futures <- yc_brl_with_futures_get(refdate) |>
  filter(!is.na(r_252), !is.na(symbol)) |>
  distinct(biz_days, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  select(refdate, forward_date, biz_days, r_252, symbol) |>
  arrange(biz_days)
futures <- bind_rows(b3 |> slice(1), futures)
```

```{r echo=FALSE}
# Saved output of the chunk above, so the vignette doesn't download data
refdate <- as.Date("2026-09-11")
data <- readRDS("b3-curve-2026-09-11.rds")
b3 <- data$b3
futures <- data$futures
```

B3's curve has `r nrow(b3)` vertices and the DI1 curve has
`r nrow(futures)`.

```{r}
head(as.data.frame(futures))
```

## The two curves

The DI1 curve gets a flat forward interpolation.

```{r}
di1_curve <- spotratecurve(
  futures$r_252, futures$biz_days,
  "discrete", "business/252", "Brazil/ANBIMA",
  refdate = refdate
)
interpolation(di1_curve) <- interp_flatforward()
di1_curve
```

B3's curve is created the same way, without interpolation: we only need its
rates.

```{r}
b3_curve <- spotratecurve(
  b3$r_252, b3$biz_days,
  "discrete", "business/252", "Brazil/ANBIMA",
  refdate = refdate
)
```

With `[[` the DI1 curve is interpolated at the terms of B3's curve, so both
curves have rates for the same terms.

```{r}
interp_curve <- di1_curve[[b3_curve@terms]]
```

```{r fig.height=4.5}
plot(as.numeric(b3_curve@terms), as.numeric(b3_curve) * 100,
  type = "l", xlab = "Business days", ylab = "Rate (%)",
  main = paste("PRE curve", refdate)
)
lines(as.numeric(b3_curve@terms), as.numeric(interp_curve) * 100,
  col = "blue", lty = 2
)
points(futures$biz_days, futures$r_252 * 100, pch = 19, col = "red", cex = 0.6)
legend("bottomright",
  c("B3", "flat forward", "DI1 vertices"),
  col = c("black", "blue", "red"), lty = c(1, 2, NA), pch = c(NA, NA, 19)
)
```

The red points are the DI1 vertices.
At this scale the curves can't be told apart, so let's look at the
differences.

## The differences

The difference between the curves is measured in basis points (bps): one
basis point is 0.01%.

```{r}
diff_bps <- (as.numeric(interp_curve) - as.numeric(b3_curve)) * 1e4
summary(diff_bps)
```

```{r fig.height=4}
plot(as.numeric(b3_curve@terms), diff_bps,
  type = "h",
  xlab = "Business days", ylab = "Difference (bps)",
  main = "fixedincome flat forward minus B3",
  ylim = c(-0.1, 0.1)
)
abline(h = c(-0.05, 0.05), lty = 2, col = "gray")
points(as.numeric(futures$biz_days), rep(0, nrow(futures)), pch = 19, col = "red", cex = 0.6)
```

The largest difference is `r sprintf("%.3f", max(abs(diff_bps), na.rm = TRUE))`
bps.
B3 publishes the rates with 5 decimal places, so each rate is rounded to
0.1 bps and the rounding error is up to 0.05 bps: the dashed lines.
All differences are inside these lines, which means that `interp_flatforward()`
gives the same curve as B3, apart from the rounding.
At the DI1 vertices (the red points) both curves have the same rates, so the
difference is zero.

The table shows the rates at a few vertices between two DI1 maturities.

```{r}
terms <- as.numeric(b3_curve@terms)
between <- which(!(terms %in% futures$biz_days) & terms < max(futures$biz_days))
idx <- between[c(10, 50, 100, 150, 190)]
data.frame(
  biz_days = as.numeric(b3_curve@terms)[idx],
  b3 = as.numeric(b3_curve)[idx],
  flatforward = round(as.numeric(interp_curve)[idx], 5),
  diff_bps = round(diff_bps[idx], 3)
)
```

Rounding the interpolated rates to 5 decimal places gives B3's rates.

## After the last DI1 contract

The last DI1 contract on this date has
`r max(futures$biz_days)` business days, but B3's curve goes up to
`r max(b3$biz_days)` business days.
`fixedincome` doesn't extrapolate, so the interpolated curve has `NA` for
these terms.

```{r}
sum(is.na(as.numeric(interp_curve)))
tail(as.data.frame(b3), 3)
```

These are the `NA` values in the summary above.
